glossary.malignant: Cancerous: able to invade nearby tissue and spread to distant sites.
glossary.bronchial epithelium: The layer of cells lining the airways (bronchi).
glossary.metastasis: Spread of cancer from where it started to a distant part of the body.
glossary.local invasion: Growth of a tumour directly into the surrounding tissues.
glossary.radiotherapy: Treatment using high-energy radiation to kill cancer cells.
glossary.dyspnoea: Shortness of breath or difficulty breathing.
glossary.night sweats: Heavy sweating at night, a classic sign of cancer, TB or lymphoma.
glossary.raised platelets: Thrombocytosis: a high platelet count, which can be a reaction to cancer.
glossary.red flag: A symptom that suggests a serious cause and needs urgent investigation.
glossary.cervical sympathetic plexus: The network of sympathetic nerves in the neck that supplies the eye and face.
glossary.sympathetic chain: A string of nerve ganglia running beside the spine carrying sympathetic nerves.
glossary.brachial plexus: The network of nerves from the neck that supplies the arm.
glossary.brachial neuropathy: Damage to the nerves of the brachial plexus causing arm pain, weakness or numbness.
glossary.hoarseness: A rough, weak voice, here from damage to the nerve supplying the vocal cords.
glossary.superior vena cava: The large vein returning blood from the head, neck and arms to the heart.
glossary.inspiratory stridor: A high-pitched noise on breathing in, caused by a narrowed upper airway.
glossary.gynaecomastia: Enlargement of breast tissue in a male.
glossary.cavitating lesion: A lesion whose centre has died and broken down, leaving an air-filled hole.
glossary.intercellular bridges: Junctions between squamous cells seen on microscopy, a sign of squamous differentiation.
glossary.poorly differentiated: Cancer cells that look little like the tissue they came from, usually meaning aggressive behaviour.
glossary.perihilar: Around the hilum, where the bronchi and vessels enter the lung.
glossary.ectopic: Produced in an abnormal place, here hormones made by tumour cells rather than their usual gland.
glossary.Cushing's syndrome: Illness from too much cortisol: weight gain, thin skin, high glucose and blood pressure.
glossary.proximal weakness: Weakness of muscles near the trunk, such as the hips and shoulders.
glossary.fibre-optic bronchoscopy: A thin flexible camera passed into the airways to look and take biopsies.
glossary.biopsy: Removal of a small piece of tissue to examine under the microscope.
glossary.contrast-enhanced CT: A CT scan after IV dye, which makes vessels and tumours stand out.
glossary.staging: Working out how big a cancer is and how far it has spread, to guide treatment.
glossary.nodule: A small round spot in the lung under 3 cm, which may be benign or malignant.
glossary.surveillance: Repeating scans over time to watch for change rather than treating straight away.
glossary.pulmonary function tests: Breathing tests measuring lung volumes and airflow, done to check fitness for surgery.
glossary.vocal cord paralysis: Loss of movement of a vocal cord, often from recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion.
glossary.chemotherapy: Drug treatment that kills rapidly dividing cancer cells.
glossary.targeted therapy: Drugs aimed at a specific mutation or protein in the cancer, such as EGFR.
glossary.immunotherapy: Treatment helping the immune system recognise and attack cancer cells.
glossary.tumour markers: Features of a tumour, such as mutations or proteins, that predict response to specific drugs.
glossary.SVC stent: A metal mesh tube placed inside the superior vena cava to hold it open.
glossary.0.9% sodium chloride: Normal saline: the standard IV fluid, used to rehydrate and help flush out calcium.
glossary.palliative care: Care focused on comfort and quality of life when a disease cannot be cured.
glossary.carcinogen: A substance that can cause cancer.
glossary.radon: A natural radioactive gas from the ground that can build up in homes and cause lung cancer.
glossary.malignant transformation: The change of a normal cell into a cancer cell through accumulated mutations.
glossary.necrosis: Death of cells or tissue, here from the tumour outgrowing its blood supply.
glossary.neuroendocrine cells: Cells that release hormones in response to nerve signals; small cell cancer arises from them.
glossary.ADH: Antidiuretic hormone: makes the kidneys hold on to water.
glossary.autoantibody: An antibody that attacks the body's own tissues.
glossary.venous return: The flow of blood back to the heart through the veins.
